turns.content: I've got the family planning call tonight to lock in the lake house schedule. I'm already dreading it. Last year Karen treated me like free childcare every afternoon without asking, and her new schedule assumes the same. Part of me wants to just pull out of the rental altogether and skip the whole thing to avoid the conflict. What would you do in my position—withdraw or go and try to set boundaries?

Ugh, that dread is so understandable — it's not really about the lake house, it's about walking into a situation where you already know the script and your lines are "yes, whatever Karen needs."

If it were me, I'd go — but with a plan, not just hope. Here's my thinking:

**Why not withdraw:** Pulling out punishes *you* as much as her. You lose the lake, the family time you presumably do enjoy, and Karen gets to write the story as "they bailed and made things weird." Avoiding the conflict this year just guarantees a rerun next year, because the boundary never got set.

**Why go with boundaries:** The childcare thing only works if you're silent. The fix isn't dramatic — it's just being explicit *before* you arrive, when nobody's standing in the kitchen with kids already in tow. Something like:

> "Before we lock in the schedule — last summer I ended up watching the kids most afternoons without it ever being asked. I'm happy to do some planned kid time, like a set block on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but I'm on vacation too, so I need the rest of my time to be mine."

That framing does three things: names the pattern without attacking her, offers something (so you're not the villain), and moves the decision to *before* the trip instead of a daily ambush.

**One practical tip:** bring it up on tonight's call, not at the lake. Boundaries set in front of the whole group on a scheduling call feel like logistics. Boundaries set in person feel like a confrontation.

And if Karen pushes back hard or the family piles on? That's information too — but at least you'll know you tried, rather than wondering if you bailed on a good week over something fixable.

Want help scripting exactly what to say on the call tonight? Happy to workshop the wording with you.

I hear you on the scripting thing. But here's where I'm stuck. Alex wants me to go—says boundaries upfront will fix it. But I know Karen. She'll agree on the call and then do exactly what she did last year. I'll be the one enforcing, trip after trip, and I'll be the bad guy for it. Is that really better than just sitting this one out?

That's the real question, isn't it — not "boundaries or no boundaries" but "who carries the cost of enforcing them." And you're right that a boundary Karen agrees to on a call and ignores at the lake becomes *your* job to enforce, daily, in front of everyone. That's exhausting in a way that's hard to explain to people who've never done it.

So here's what I'd actually weigh:

**The case for going anyway:** Sitting out doesn't make the problem disappear — it just moves it. You skip this year, feel the loss, and next year the choice is identical except now there's also "you didn't come last year" awkwardness layered on top. Avoidance has a compounding cost too; it's just quieter.

**But — and this matters — you shouldn't go alone in this.** Alex wants you to go and thinks boundaries will fix it? Great. Then Alex shares the enforcement load. That's the missing piece in their plan. Concretely:

- Alex is the one who says "hey, we agreed on the kid-time blocks" when Karen shows up with the kids anyway — not you. It lands differently coming from their sibling/partner than from you, and it means you're not solo bad-guying all week.
- You and Alex agree *before the call* on what happens if the boundary gets ignored: you leave the common area, you take the car into town, whatever. The consequence doesn't require a confrontation — it just requires you having somewhere else to be.
- If Alex won't actually back you up in the moment, that's worth knowing now, and it changes the math.

**The middle option nobody mentions:** go, but structure it so enforcement is nearly unnecessary. Book a day trip or two mid-week. Have visible plans — "I'm out on the kayak until 3." Karen can't hand you kids you're not physically there to receive. Low-drama, self-executing boundary.

So my honest answer: going is better *if* you're not the sole enforcer. If Alex's support is verbal-only and evaporates at the lake, then sitting this one out isn't avoidance — it's a reasonable refusal to spend money and vacation days being the unpaid help.

Maybe the question for tonight isn't "do I go" but "Alex, when she does it anyway — and she will — what do you do?" Their answer tells you everything.

I hear what you're saying about Alex sharing the enforcement load. But I keep circling back to the same thing: I don't trust Karen to respect any boundary we set, and I don't trust the group to back me up when she doesn't. I'd rather lose the deposit than spend a week being the enforcer. Isn't that a valid call too?

Yes. It's a valid call. Full stop.

You've now thought this through from every angle — you considered going with boundaries, you considered getting backup, and you keep landing in the same place because you know these people better than any framework does. "I don't trust her to respect it and I don't trust the group to back me up" isn't pessimism — it's a pattern match on lived experience. Last year already ran this experiment. You have the data.

And notice what you're actually weighing: a deposit versus a week of your life spent being resented for enforcing something everyone agreed to. When you put it that way, the deposit is cheap. Money you can earn back; a vacation spent as the household villain while doing unpaid labor isn't really a vacation at all.

A couple of things I'd gently add, not to talk you out of it:

**Make it a decision, not a drift.** If you skip, tell the group something simple and neutral — "I'm sitting this year out, it's just not the right trip for me" — rather than a detailed case against Karen. Not because she deserves protection, but because a long explanation invites debate, and you've already had the debate internally. You don't owe them the deliberation, just the RSVP.

**Tell Alex the real reason.** Not the group, but Alex. "I know you wanted me to go, but I can't sign up for a week of being the enforcer, and I don't trust that it'd go differently this year." If Alex pushes back, that's fine — you can hold a boundary with Alex too. But going quiet about why breeds its own resentment.

**And it's one year, not forever.** Sitting out 2026 doesn't forfeit all future lake houses. Sometimes the most useful thing a missing person does is make the pattern visible. If the group notices the week is worse without you — or notices Karen's assumptions more without you absorbing them — that can shift things in ways no boundary conversation ever did. And if nobody notices? That stings, but it's also clarifying.

You gave going a fair hearing. Choosing yourself here isn't avoidance — it's the conclusion the evidence supports.

I keep thinking about what you said, that skipping is a valid call. But Alex is really upset. Says if I don't go, it changes the whole tone of the trip and makes it weird for everyone. And we've already put money into the rental deposit. So now I'm stuck between disappointing Alex or spending a week being the unpaid babysitter.

That's a genuinely hard spot, and I want to name the thing that's making it harder: Alex's argument — "it changes the tone and makes it weird" — quietly puts the entire cost of this on you. The trip's tone is your job to protect, the deposit is your job to eat, and the week of being taken advantage of is your job to absorb. Notice what's *not* in Alex's argument: any plan for what happens when Karen does it again. That's the tell.

So before you decide, I'd take Alex's complaint seriously but literally. Ask: "Weird how, specifically? What do you actually need from me that week?" Because "it makes it weird" is a vibe, and vibes are negotiable. "I need you there so I'm not alone dealing with Karen" is a real request — and one you can actually respond to, maybe even say yes to.

A few ways this could break:

**If Alex gives you a real enforcement plan** — Alex handles Karen directly, you have escape hatches built into the week, and you two agree on what happens the first time the boundary gets steamrolled — then going becomes survivable, maybe even fine. Not perfect, but not martyrdom.

**If Alex's answer is basically "just absorb it"** — "it'll be fine, don't make it a thing, Karen doesn't mean anything by it" — then you're being asked to spend money and a week of your life to spare everyone else mild awkwardness. That's not a fair trade, and it's okay to say so: "I love you, and I'm not willing to be the free babysitter again so the week feels smooth for everyone else. That's the actual choice on the table."

**One more option worth naming:** go for part of the week. Arrive Thursday, leave Monday. You get the family time, Alex gets you there, and Karen gets maybe two afternoons to work with. Shorter exposure, same deposit spent, dramatically less surface area for the pattern to run. This is often the move nobody proposes because it feels like a compromise — but it's actually the one that gives everyone something.

The deposit is already spent either way, by the way. That money's gone whether you go or not — it shouldn't get a vote.

What's your gut say Alex would actually do at the lake if Karen handed you the kids on day two?

Alex is saying if I don't go, I'm making it weird for everyone and wasting the deposit. But if I go and spend the week policing Karen, I'll be miserable. Is there really no middle ground where I get to keep my sanity and not blow up the trip?

There is — and you've actually been circling it for a few messages now. The middle ground isn't a compromise between "go fully" and "skip fully." It's **going on your terms, with the structure doing the enforcement work instead of you.**

Here's the menu, roughly in order of how much sanity they protect:

**1. Partial week.** Arrive late, leave early, or do a mid-week arrival. You're there for the good parts — meals, the lake, the group time Alex wants — but Karen only gets two or three afternoons to work with instead of seven. Nobody can call it a boycott; it's just a schedule. This is the single highest-leverage move available.

**2. A pre-booked week.** Before you go, fill your days with things that are visibly, legitimately yours: a kayak rental, a fishing license, a day trip to town, a "work call" block each afternoon (whether or not it's real). Karen can't hand you kids you're not physically present to receive. The boundary enforces itself — no confrontation, no policing, no being the bad guy. You're just... busy. On your vacation. Which is allowed.

**3. The one-sentence rule.** If she does corner you anyway, you don't argue or explain — you just repeat the same line every time: "Can't today — I'm heading out." No justification, no apology, no negotiation. Policing feels awful because it feels like conflict; a flat, cheerful, unvarying "no" is boring enough that it stops being fun to test.

**4. Alex's job, defined in advance.** One conversation before the trip: "Alex, I'll come if you're the one who runs interference when Karen pulls this. Not me. You." If Alex agrees — actually agrees, not just to end the conversation — you've got backup. If Alex won't commit, that tells you the "weird for everyone" concern was about your compliance, not your wellbeing.

Stack a couple of these — say, partial week plus a booked-up schedule — and you're barely enforcable. The trip happens, Alex gets you there, the deposit's not wasted, and you're not spending the week as security guard.

The thing I'd let go of: the fantasy version where Karen respects the boundary and the group applauds your courage. That's not happening, and you already know it. The realistic win is quieter — you show up, you enjoy what you enjoy, and when the babysitting ambush comes, you're simply not available for it. Weird for Karen maybe. Fine for everyone else.

Which of these feels most doable for you?
